newsitem.title: UK: Treasuries edge up in London, auction seen well bid.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries edge up in London, auction seen well bid.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries were slightly better bid in London on Wednesday with one or two big trades driving the market ahead of the $12.0 billion 10-year note auction later, traders said.

They said the 10-year paper would likely come under some pressure at the New York open as investors knock the market back in preparation for the sale. But they added the latest leg of the quarterly refunding was expected to go reasonably well.

"The auction should go pretty well," said one trader. "The 10-year paper should be in a fairly compelling region for real money to step in and buy the market after the pretty severe correction we've had in the last few days."
The quarterly refunding continues on Thursday with the $10 billion sale of 30-year bonds.

By 1007 GMT, 10-year notes were at 102-25 to yield 6.24 percent, up from 102-22 in Tokyo but off from 102-26 at the New York close. The 30-year long bond was at 101-21 to yield 6.5 percent, up from 101-16 in Tokyo but still down from the 101-24 New York close.

Rob Hayward, economic adviser at Bank America, said as long as the Federal Reserve's Beige Book, due 1800 GMT, did not throw up any nasty surprises on inflation, the market may enjoy a small bounce after the auction.
"I imagine traders will try and get a bit of a concession before the sale, and they will probably be successful in that," he said.
"But I think the auction will be O.K. and after that I think we'll have a bit of a bounce."
Hayward said the Beige Book, the Fed's anecdotal account of business conditions around the nation, would reaffirm the expectation the Fed will leave interest rates on hold in August.

"In the last few Beige Books labour market conditions have tightened, but there's been no mention of any wage pressures -- and the recent employment report and ECI (Employment Cost Index) seem to say that remains the case," he said.
"So it will reaffirm the idea that although the economy is picking up in the third quarter, for the time being there doesn't seem to be any need for the Fed to change rates," said Hayward.
By 1015 GMT, September T-bond futures were down 3/32 at 114-16.
